{{Short description|Formula that relates characteristics of the pipe and internal pressure it can withstand}}
'''Barlow's formula''' (called "Kesselformel"<ref>{{Citation| title=Kesselformel| date=2025-07-06| url=https://de.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kesselformel&oldid=257665617| work=Wikipedia| language=de| access-date=2025-07-06}}</ref> in German) relates the internal pressure that a [[pipe (material)|pipe]]<ref>Or pressure vessel, or other cylindrical pressure containment structure.</ref> can withstand to its dimensions and the [[Strength of materials|strength of its material]].

This approximate formula is named after [[Peter Barlow (mathematician)|Peter Barlow]], an English [[mathematician]].<ref>{{cite conference
  |url= https://onepetro.org/SPEDC/proceedings-abstract/18DC/3-18DC/D031S013R001/214112
  |title= The Barlow Equation for Tubular Burst: A Muddled History
  |last1= Adams  |first1=A.J.
  |last2= Grundy |first2=K.C.
  |last3= Lin    |first3=B.
  |last4= Moore  |first4=PW.
  |date= 6 March 2018
  |pages=  SPE-189681-MS
  |location= Fort Worth, Texas, USA
  |conference= IADC/SPE Drilling Conference and Exhibition
  |doi=10.2118/189681-MS|url-access= subscription
  }}</ref>

:<math>P=\frac {2 \sigma_\theta s} {D}</math>[[File:Zylindersegment mit Maßen.png|thumb|252x252px|Cylinder]],

where

:<math>P</math>  : internal pressure,
:<math>\sigma_\theta</math> : [[Strength of materials|allowable]] [[Cylinder stress#Hoop stress|stress]],
:<math>s</math>   : wall thickness,
:<math>D</math> : outside diameter.

This formula (DIN 2413) figures prominently in the design of [[Autoclave (industrial)|autoclaves]] and other [[Pressure vessel#Stress in thin-walled pressure vessels|pressure vessels]].

==Other formulations==

The design of a complex pressure containment system involves much more than the application of Barlow's formula. For example, in 100 countries the [[ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code|ASME BPVC]] stipulates the requirements for design and testing of [[pressure vessel]]s.<ref>{{Cite web
  | title =  2017 Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code: An International Code
  | access-date = 9 October 2021
  | url = https://www.asme.org/getmedia/c041390f-6d23-4bf9-a953-646127cfbd51/asme-bpvc-brochure-webview.pdf}}</ref>

The formula is also common in the pipeline industry to verify that pipe used for gathering, transmission, and distribution lines can safely withstand operating pressures. The design factor is multiplied by the resulting pressure which gives the maximum operating pressure (MAOP) for the pipeline. In the United States, this design factor is dependent on Class locations which are defined in [[US Department of Transportation|DOT]] Part 192. There are four class locations corresponding to four design factors:<ref>{{Cite web
  | title =  US Code of Regulations: Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 192.5
  | access-date = 9 October 2021
  | url = https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-192#192.5}}</ref>

{|class="wikitable"
!Class
!width=700|Definition
!Design<br>factor
|-
|1||An offshore area or any class location unit that has 10 or fewer buildings intended for human occupancy||0.72
|-
|2||Any class location that has more than 10 but fewer than 46 buildings intended for human occupancy||0.60
|-
|3||Any location that has 46 or more buildings intended for human occupancy or any area where the pipeline lies within 100 yards (91 meters) of a building or a small, well-defined outdoor area (such as a playground, recreation area, outdoor theater, or place of public assembly) that is occupied by 20 or more persons at least five days a week for 10 weeks in any 12-month period—weeks need not be consecutive||0.50
|-
|4||Any class location unit where buildings with four or more stories above the ground are prevalent||0.40
|}
